Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings: Acute onset watery diarrhea, intermittent LLQ cramps, initial vomiting, subjective fever; onset within 24 h of takeaway meal; no blood in stool or vomit; able to maintain hydration; PMH asthma only; no red-flag features (persistent vomiting, severe dehydration, bleeding).

Working diagnosis: Acute gastroenteritis, likely viral; bacterial food-borne infection less likely but possible.

Differential diagnoses (consistent with DDx):  
• Acute viral gastroenteritis – High likelihood: abrupt onset, household contact vomited, self-limiting pattern.  
• Acute bacterial food-borne infection (Salmonella/Campylobacter/ETEC) – Moderate likelihood: restaurant exposure, abdominal cramps, subjective fever.  
• Diverticulitis with secondary diarrhea – Low likelihood given age, transient pain, large-volume watery stools.

Management Plan

- Conservative management explained and agreed.  
- Oral rehydration: advised use of commercial ORS (e.g., Dioralyte) and adequate fluid intake.  
- Symptomatic relief: paracetamol 1 g (two 500 mg tablets) up to four times daily as needed (exact dose/frequency advised verbally).  
- Rest and sick leave: recommended 2–3 days off work.  
- Red-flag advice: return or seek care if diarrhea >3–4 days, bloody stool, high fever, worsening pain, inability to keep fluids down.  
- Follow-up: review in 3–4 days if not improving; consider stool culture and blood tests at that time.  
- Patient verbalized understanding; no further questions.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):

1. Acute viral gastroenteritis – High: classic self-limiting triad (watery diarrhea, vomiting, low-grade fever) and household contact vomit.  
2. Acute bacterial food-borne infection – Moderate: onset after takeaway meal; abdominal cramps/feverish feeling.  
3. Diverticulitis – Low: left-sided pain; age and stool volume make this less likely.
